content: Between 2010 and 2014, nearly 600 million adults aged 15 and older accessed HIV testing services in 122 lowand middle-income countries. In 2014 alone, approximately 150 million children, men, and women in 129 lowand middle-income countries received HIV testing and their results. This significant scale-up was made possible, in part, by the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), which have been critical in expanding HIV testing services (HTS), especially in resource-limited settings where laboratory access is restricted. RDTs prequalified by the World Health Organization (WHO) demonstrate a diagnostic sensitivity of at least 99% and a specificity of 98%. When used within a WHO-recommended testing strategy and a validated national testing algorithm, these RDTs have shown high reliability. However, many countries have not implemented quality management systems that align with the scale-up of HTS. They have also failed to utilize WHO-prequalified RDTs or adopt WHO-recommended testing strategies. A recent analysis of HIV testing policies in 48 countries revealed that only 20% of testing strategies adhered to current WHO recommendations. Reports of poor-quality HIV testing are increasing, with some cases leading to misdiagnosis of HIV status—either falsely identifying an HIV-positive individual as negative or vice versa. Audits in certain settings have revealed substantial rates of false-positive diagnoses. Misdiagnosis can result from assay limitations, operator errors, facility-related issues (e.g., improper reagent storage or inappropriate testing strategies), and suboptimal national testing algorithms. Additionally, high client volumes leading to overburdened staff or low client volumes resulting in poor proficiency, inadequate training, and lack of supportive supervision contribute to operator errors. In many countries, errors often go undetected and uncorrected due to the absence of comprehensive quality management systems or external quality assessments. The consequences of misdiagnosis are severe. A false-negative HIV status represents a failure to correctly diagnose a client, link them to prevention, treatment, and care services, and prevent ongoing HIV transmission. Conversely, a false-positive diagnosis can lead to unnecessary initiation of lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART), stigma, discrimination, and even criminalization. It also limits the availability of interventions to prevent HIV infection, harms community and family relationships, and undermines trust in health services if the error is later discovered. Incorrectly initiating ART wastes valuable resources, including medication stocks, clinic time, and laboratory monitoring. This issue is particularly concerning in settings where clients are offered immediate ART initiation after receiving an HIV-positive result, regardless of CD4 count or clinical assessment. If left unaddressed, these quality issues and misdiagnoses could undermine global HIV response efforts and hinder progress toward achieving targets such as diagnosing 90% of people with HIV by 2020, preventing new infections, and providing treatment to those living with HIV. To better understand the causes and extent of HIV misdiagnosis, a systematic literature review was conducted. This review assessed factors contributing to misdiagnosis in various settings. The search strategy included scientific databases, conference abstracts, and government and NGO websites, focusing on terms related to misclassification, testing errors, and quality assurance. Studies were included if they reported on errors such as clerical/technical mistakes, user errors, cross-reactivity, suboptimal testing strategies, or poor management and supervision. The review followed PRISMA reporting standards, and data were extracted and verified by multiple reviewers. The review identified several key factors contributing to HIV misdiagnosis. These include poor management of supplies (e.g., use of damaged or expired test kits), user errors in interpreting weak reactive test results, and reliance on a tiebreaker testing strategy. Poor management of supplies was reported in half of the studies addressing management and supervision issues. Inadequate training and certification of staff providing HIV testing services were also common, with some studies highlighting the involvement of ineligible providers. User errors were frequently reported, including incorrect specimen collection, misinterpretation of test results, and reliance on a single assay to issue an HIV-positive diagnosis. Weak test lines or bands were often over-interpreted as reactive, leading to false-positive diagnoses. Studies also noted that faint test lines were more likely to result in incorrect HIV-positive diagnoses. For example, a study from Uganda found that most false-reactive results were associated with weak test lines on one or more RDTs. Similarly, a study from the UK reported that false-reactive specimens often had fainter test lines compared to true-positive specimens. Suboptimal testing strategies, such as the use of a tiebreaker approach, were linked to high rates of false-positive results. For instance, studies from Uganda reported false-positive rates of 43.7% and 48.2% when using a tiebreaker strategy. Poor management and supervision practices, including the use of damaged or expired test kits, stock-outs, and inadequate adherence to standard operating procedures, were also significant contributors to misdiagnosis. In some cases, non-laboratory personnel were found to be using incorrect tests, such as syphilis RDTs, to diagnose HIV infections. The review highlighted the need for comprehensive quality management systems, including external quality assessments, to detect and correct errors. Without such systems, errors may go unnoticed, leading to serious consequences for individuals and communities. Addressing these issues is critical to ensuring the accuracy of HIV testing, maintaining trust in health services, and achieving global HIV targets.
